items.abstract: <jats:p>Financial sectors are highly connected, and those relationships can change quickly when market conditions change. Graph neural networks (GNNs) are one way to model these relationships directly, but it is not clear whether a dynamic market graph actually improves short-term forecasting compared with models that already receive the same sector information. This paper tests whether dynamic sector-correlation networks improve five-trading-day direction prediction for U.S. equity sectors. Nine sector exchange-traded funds are represented as nodes, with edges created from rolling return correlations. To avoid using the final test period when choosing the graph, the correlation window and threshold are selected using data before 2015. A 20-trading-day window and 0.70 correlation threshold are then used in the final experiment. Random Forest and multilayer perceptron (MLP) baselines are compared with target-aware Graph Attention Network (GAT) and GraphSAGE models for financials (XLF), industrials (XLI), and technology (XLK). Final evaluation uses expanding-window walk-forward testing from 2015 through June 2, 2026, with a five-session purge at each train-test boundary. The network changes substantially during stressed markets. Average sector correlation increases from 0.533 during low-volatility periods to 0.724 during high-volatility periods, while network density rises from 0.358 to 0.656. Similar changes appear between bull and bear markets. However, the GNN models do not consistently outperform the non-graph baselines. Pooled out-of-sample AUCs remain between about 0.51 and 0.54. GraphSAGE performs best for XLI, while the MLP performs best for XLF and XLK. All paired moving-block bootstrap confidence intervals comparing model AUCs include zero. The results show that sector networks become much more connected during stressed markets, but those stronger relationships do not provide a reliable predictive advantage to the tested GNN models. The correlation graph appears more useful for describing changes in market structure than for improving five-day sector direction forecasts.</jats:p>
